clue.text: This unit, however, is not specially employed on looting operations

definitions.text: This unit, however, is not specially employed on looting operations

parts.words: This unit, however, is not specially employed on looting operations
parts.note: to rifle is to loot or ransack, so a unit named for rifling might be expected to plunder; this infantry regiment is named for its rifles

explanation.surface: A wry military note insisting a certain regiment is not, despite its name, a band of plunderers.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the second sense of 'rifle': to ransack. The regiment takes its name from the firearm, not from looting.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rifle Brigade was a famous British Army infantry regiment, so it is a military unit.

clue.text: Arrive logically at a negative conclusion

definitions.text: Arrive logically at a negative conclusion

indicators.note: conclusion says the negative piece comes at the end of the word

parts.note: to infer is to reach a conclusion by reasoning
no is the negative answer

explanation.surface: Reasoning one's way to a gloomy outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: inferring and then adding a negative at the end builds the word, and hell is the most negative conclusion a life can reach.
explanation.definitionFit: An inferno is hell, the worst possible end, which the clue jokingly calls a negative conclusion.

definitions.note: a plural pronoun standing for the plural answer

indicators.note: might be says the two words could become something else once their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A suggestion that some vessels could be out at sea under canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of UNDER SAIL rearranged give the answer; the definition is just 'They', a cheeky blank for whatever the anagram makes.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun simply stands in for the plural noun: washhouses, the places that wash clothes.

parts.note: but can mean only, as in 'but a child'
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: A dismissive remark that something is merely a curl of hair.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no separate definition: the clue is pure wordplay, with the whole presented as if it described a flimsy support, the opposite of the sturdy wall prop it makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A buttress is a mass of masonry built against a wall to support it, a prop far from flimsy.

clue.text: Where one is proverbially recommended to "go native "

definitions.text: Where one is proverbially recommended to "go native "

parts.words: Where one is proverbially recommended to "go native "
parts.note: the proverb says when visiting the Italian capital, do as its people do, which is going native

explanation.surface: A question about the place where a proverb tells travellers to adopt local ways.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb 'When in Rome, do as the Romans do' advises adopting local customs, so the place is the Italian capital.

indicators.note: a loose signal: the range is made with the letters of the following two words, shuffled

explanation.surface: A mountain chain described as having a tail.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is barely there: 'with' merely says the range is made with the letters of 'a tail', rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The Altai are a mountain range in Central Asia where Russia, China, Mongolia and Kazakhstan meet.

parts.note: something useful for an end in view, a means that does the job

explanation.surface: A plain remark that something ought to do the job.
explanation.definitionFit: An expedient is a means of achieving a particular end, often a convenient stopgap.

clue.text: State that makes a girl cry

parts.note: Ida is a girl's name
ho is a cry, to attract attention, as in 'land ho'

explanation.surface: Speaks of some circumstance that reduces a young woman to tears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a condition or mood that makes her weep; it is a US state, and 'cry' is a shout, not tears.
explanation.definitionFit: Idaho is one of the states of the USA, in the north-west.

parts.note: a Black Maria is a police van that takes people back into custody, a going back in

explanation.surface: Just a query about a police van.
explanation.walkthrough: The van offers a 're-gress': where an egress is a way out, the police van is the way back in.
explanation.definitionFit: To regress is to go back; the van carries offenders back inside, a return the clue plays on.

indicators.note: the abbreviation for anagram tells the solver to rearrange the three preceding words

explanation.surface: A bare instruction naming a scarlet wind instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Times puzzles sometimes gave a straight anagram with no definition at all; the solver had only the letters and the crossings to go on.
explanation.definitionFit: A defaulter is one who fails to pay a debt or appear when required, which no clue word defines here.

clue.text: Work in a sand hill goes to the head

definitions.note: a phrase for something worn on the head, for the noun answer

indicators.note: in says the work sits inside the sand hill

parts.note: a golf tee was once a small heap of sand
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Labour on a dune that ends up making someone light-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes to the head' suggests intoxication; here it is simply what a hat does. Golf tees were once little mounds of sand.
explanation.definitionFit: A topee is a light pith helmet worn in hot climates, so it sits on one's head.

indicators.note: without asks for the letters of assistance to be removed from the other words

parts.note: aid means assistance

explanation.surface: A hero achieved something on their own.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of AID are taken out scattered: the opening A, then the I and D of 'did'.
explanation.definitionFit: Herod was the Judean king of the Gospels, ironically the opposite of a hero, so no clue word truly defines him.

parts.note: unsold books discarded cheaply by a publisher, not albums of cuttings

explanation.surface: A distinction between waste books and albums of clippings.
explanation.definitionFit: Remainders are a publisher's unsold stock sold off cheaply or pulped, books treated as scrap.

clue.text: Strange that mendacity in a multitude should prove to be this

definitions.text: Strange that mendacity in a multitude should prove to be this

indicators.note: in says the mendacity is set within the multitude

parts.note: a host is a multitude, a great number
mendacity is lying, a lie

explanation.surface: A paradox: a crowd full of falsehood turning out to be supremely pure.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well as the wordplay: it is strange that a lie inside a host should produce the most sacred thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Holiest means most sacred or saintly, the strange opposite of lying.

clue.text: "Save where the beetle- his droning flight" (Gray)

definitions.text: "Save where the beetle- his droning flight" (Gray)

parts.words: "Save where the beetle- his droning flight" (Gray)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard

explanation.surface: A line from Gray's Elegy with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Gray's line reads 'Save where the beetle wheels his droning flight', the insect circling in the dusk.

indicators.note: of to-day asks for the drain-hole in a modern, remade form, so its letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A plughole, oddly said to belong to the present day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of to-day' does two jobs: it asks for an updated version of DRAIN-HOLE, its letters reshuffled, and it is what the resulting rare word means.
explanation.definitionFit: Hodiernal is a rare word from Latin hodie, meaning relating to the present day.

parts.note: a past-tense question about a woman, reworded with a past participle in place of the verb, gives a word for an illicit Irish drinking den

explanation.surface: A short question about a woman's past.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as SHE BEEN, the word answers the question; it is in fact an Irish word for an illicit drinking den.
explanation.definitionFit: A shebeen is an unlicensed bar, chiefly in Ireland, Scotland and South Africa.

clue.text: An odd plant; it doesn't grow anywhere

parts.note: rum means odd or strange
a shrub is a plant

explanation.surface: A strange plant that refuses to grow in any soil.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'plant' is not a plant at all: this shrub is a drink of rum mixed with fruit juice and sugar, so it never grows.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum shrub is a cordial of rum, citrus juice and sugar, a drink rather than any growing thing.

indicators.note: the exclamation mark flags that the two words are not to be taken at face value but jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: Denying that a particular woman is candid.
explanation.walkthrough: The only signal is the exclamation mark, a liberty of early Times puzzles: jumble NOT SHE.
explanation.definitionFit: Honest means frank and truthful, so straightforward.

parts.note: things grasped by the mind alone, as opposed to things perceived by the senses

explanation.surface: A philosophical remark about things that live only in the mind.
explanation.definitionFit: In Kant's philosophy noumena are things as they are in themselves, knowable by intellect, not perceived as phenomena.

parts.note: a member of the bands of English workers who wrecked factory machinery in the early nineteenth century

explanation.surface: A description of one of history's first wreckers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Luddites smashed textile machines in 1811 to 1816, protesting at mechanisation, early saboteurs.

parts.note: aspirated means given an H sound at the front, so the letter H goes before
eight is a number

explanation.surface: A figure pronounced with a breath at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: To aspirate a word is to sound an H at its start; the clue has no separate definition, though a height is itself a measured number.
explanation.definitionFit: A height is a measurement of how tall something is, a figure such as eight feet.

clue.text: Not the ideal material for landings

definitions.text: Not the ideal material for landings

parts.words: Not the ideal material for landings
parts.note: a coarse linen fabric that also names a disastrous aircraft landing

explanation.surface: Advice that some fabric is a poor choice for covering stair landings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'landings' suggests carpets on stairs; the other sense is an aircraft coming down, where a crash landing is far from ideal.
explanation.definitionFit: Crash is a coarse linen cloth used for towels, and a crash landing is a bad way for an aircraft to arrive.

parts.note: the cosmos is often described as having no edge or limit

explanation.surface: A comparison with the whole cosmos.
explanation.definitionFit: Boundless means without limits, as the universe is commonly thought to be.

parts.note: a stretch of land at a river mouth, enclosed by the river's channels and the sea

explanation.surface: The schoolbook description of an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The words look like the textbook definition of an island; the answer is the alluvial land between a river's branching mouths.
explanation.definitionFit: A delta is the triangular tract of silt at a river's mouth, ringed by channels and sea.

clue.text: " It is a nipping and an — air "(Hamlet)

definitions.text: " It is a nipping and an — air "(Hamlet)

parts.words: " It is a nipping and an — air "(Hamlet)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Horatio's line on the battlements in Act 1 of Hamlet

explanation.surface: A quotation from Hamlet with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatio answers Hamlet's 'The air bites shrewdly' with 'It is a nipping and an eager air', eager meaning sharp.

clue.text: Lancaster was not the kind of man Caesar liked to have about him

definitions.meaning: John of ... was Duke of Lancaster, father of Henry IV

definitions.text: not the kind of man Caesar liked to have about him
definitions.meaning: Shakespeare's Caesar wants men about him that are fat, not lean and hungry like Cassius

explanation.surface: A historical duke compared with Julius Caesar's taste in companions.
explanation.walkthrough: In Julius Caesar, Caesar says 'Let me have men about me that are fat' and distrusts Cassius's 'lean and hungry look'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaunt means thin and haggard, the lean look Caesar mistrusted, and is also the duke's surname.

clue.text: Where sheep can be counted by fifties

definitions.note: a place, for the place-name answer

parts.note: a ewe is a female sheep
L is the Roman numeral for fifty, so two of them are two fifties

explanation.surface: A spot where a flock is tallied fifty at a time.
explanation.walkthrough: Ewell is a town in Surrey, near Epsom, south-west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Ewell is a town in Surrey, England, so it answers the question of where.

indicators.note: flowery language is ornate and elaborated, so the hyphenated phrase is dressed up into a new order of its letters

explanation.surface: An ornate description of a mine yielding sugar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowery' both signals that SUGAR-MINE is rearranged and hints at the flowering plants the letters make; the whole is a fanciful name for a bed of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Geraniums are popular flowering garden plants, a flowery source of nectar, the sugar bees mine.

clue.text: Outstanding characteristic of the Vicar of Bray

definitions.text: Outstanding characteristic of the Vicar of Bray

parts.words: Outstanding characteristic of the Vicar of Bray
parts.note: the vicar of the old song changed his religion with each new monarch to keep his living

explanation.surface: A comment on the chief trait of a famous turncoat clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: The Vicar of Bray, from an eighteenth-century English song, switched between Catholic and Protestant as each monarch required.
explanation.definitionFit: His talent was adjusting his beliefs to any regime, the quality of fitting in with changing circumstances.
